decisions.problem: Vehicle data, postcode lookup and lead submission all need third-party credentials.
decisions.decision: Proxy every call through 15 nonce-checked quote/v1 WordPress REST routes.
decisions.reasoning: No key in the JS bundle; one place for CSRF checks and payload reshaping.
decisions.tradeoffs: Extra hop and latency; WordPress becomes an availability dependency; a PHP surface to maintain alongside React.
decisions.result: Credentials stayed server-side; two vendor contract changes absorbed in PHP without a front-end release.

decisions.problem: Lead ingestion is revenue-critical and a single App Service is a single point of failure.
decisions.decision: Two thin front ends (ASP.NET Core, Azure Functions) over one shared Leads.Core.
decisions.tradeoffs: Middleware duplicated (219 vs 212 near-identical lines); every cross-cutting change made twice.
decisions.result: Redundancy achieved; maintenance cost visible in the subject's own PII and auth commits, which each touched both.

decisions.problem: An enrolment that threw after possibly creating a CRM customer.
decisions.decision: Return 'failed' with alreadyExists rather than retry when no customer ID was saved and a fail reason exists.
decisions.reasoning: Stated in the code: a failed CRM operation has an unknown external outcome.
decisions.tradeoffs: Genuinely-failed leads need human or upstream intervention.
decisions.result: No duplicate customers created in a third-party system.

decisions.problem: Marketing needed to place calculators without editing shortcode syntax.
decisions.decision: Shortcode reads an ACF field first, falls back to the attribute.
decisions.reasoning: Editor-friendly, no developer in the loop.
decisions.tradeoffs: Hidden dependency on ACF being installed and the field existing.
decisions.result: Editor-placeable calculators; existing attribute usages preserved.

decisions.problem: Identity assignment must not block lead capture.
decisions.decision: 1-second HTTP timeout on the Leela call.
decisions.tradeoffs: Leads can land without a leela_id under load.

decisions.problem: Customers abandon long insurance forms part-way through; a drop-out who has given a phone number is still a contactable lead.
decisions.decision: INHERITED: post a partial submission mid-journey, then post again in full, and let the lead API's de-duplication layer suppress the second dial.
decisions.reasoning: Captures abandoners with no change to the lead API contract: the cheapest possible implementation.
decisions.tradeoffs: Severe and measurable. One enquiry produces two rows; 48.6% of website submissions are repeat posts within 30 minutes; a third of the leads table is non-actionable; every naive COUNT(*) overstates demand; correctness depends on time-window heuristics rather than identity.
decisions.result: The subject identified this as the thing they would design differently and has already built half the fix: the newer verticals they authored generate a client-side uuidv4(), forwarded on the Marketplace data-warehouse route but not on the main lead-API route, which has no column for it. Closing the loop is bounded work: forward the field, add a nullable indexed column, upsert on it when present.

decisions.problem: The original lead ingestion service was a Go application maintained by the senior engineer; the business wanted it on a stack the wider team and the then-CTO preferred.
decisions.decision: Full C# reimplementation targeting business-logic parity with the live Go service.
decisions.reasoning: Organisational (stack consolidation, maintainability by the available team) rather than technical. The .NET choice was a CTO-level mandate; the subject would have chosen differently had the call been theirs.
decisions.tradeoffs: A rewrite of a revenue-critical service carries migration risk for no new functionality, and parity with a live system is an exacting constraint. Visible throughout the codebase: 'mirroring Go implementation' comments across multiple services, and XidGenerator hand-ported from rs/xid down to the byte layout so production IDs stay sortable.
decisions.result: The .NET service runs at ~341 leads/day with a 1.30% non-duplicate failure rate; the parity constraint was met. Implementation was predominantly the senior engineer's work; the subject's documented role is architectural participation and subsequent ownership.

problems_solved.title: Diagnosing a 33% duplicate rate as an architecture artifact
problems_solved.situation: 212,054 production rows flagged duplicate — a third of everything the platform recorded. Reads cold as a broken de-duplication layer or a lead-quality problem, and is the first thing an interviewer would challenge.
problems_solved.problem: Neither explanation is correct and the data does not volunteer the real one: no partial flag is persisted on the lead row, so partial and full submissions are indistinguishable after the fact.
problems_solved.investigation_solution: Three steps. Code: nextHandler posts a partial mid-journey, send.php forwards a partial boolean, and the leads table has no correlation-ID column, so a second post cannot be matched by identity. Timing: 94.1% of website duplicates arrive within 30 minutes of the original and 91% within five, which is not human behaviour. Control group: the website channel shows a 48.6% sub-30-minute repeat rate against 0.2-6.7% for affiliate feeds that post a single complete lead — a 240x difference.
problems_solved.result: Mechanism established beyond doubt; platform figures restated as unique enquiries (309,486 platform-wide, 77,433 website) instead of raw rows; a bounded code fix specified.
problems_solved.evidence: src/utils/index.ts nextHandler; plugin/api/functions/send.php; src/data/businessInsurance.ts:6; gap-distribution and channel-comparison tables; leads schema

problems_solved.title: Paid-search click IDs lost across a multi-step journey
problems_solved.situation: Visitor arrives with a click ID, submits several pages and minutes later.
problems_solved.problem: The ID must survive navigation, and Microsoft Ads uses msclkid not gclid.
problems_solved.investigation_solution: 30-day cookie set on init for both parameters (both written to one cookie name); theme-level script persisting the query string to localStorage; form code reading both back at submit.
problems_solved.result: 149,940 production leads carry a click ID; website coverage 63-73% in 2025-2026 vs 35.7% in 2024.

lessons.lesson: If a workflow can produce the same logical event more than once, that event's identity must be decided where it starts — in the browser, at the first keystroke — not reconstructed by the server afterwards. Deferring that decision cost years of duplicate rows, heuristic de-duplication and a caveat on every downstream count. The fix was always small; what made it expensive was that nobody had quantified the cost.

Working inside a parity constraint teaches what a greenfield build cannot: the previous system's behaviour becomes your specification, including its mistakes, and 'improve it while you port it' is usually wrong because it destroys the one thing that makes the migration verifiable.
Isolating per-vertical configuration (data/types/validation modules) from shared presentation components made twelve verticals tractable; new verticals reached production within days.
Proxying third-party calls through WordPress kept credentials out of the bundle and absorbed two vendor contract changes without a front-end release.
A stable fail_reason taxonomy is the reason a reliability figure could be produced at all; without it duplicates and genuine failures would be indistinguishable.
Secret management was reactive; credentials reached the repository and took three commits to clear. Pre-commit scanning and key rotation are the actual fix.
Duplicating middleware across two hosts has cost real effort on every cross-cutting change.
Shipping a dialler timing change before confirming it with the business cost a ship-revert-reship cycle.
External systems fail partially; the correct response is often to stop rather than retry.
Logging usefully and logging safely are in genuine tension and need a deliberate design, not a log-level change.
Extract duplicated middleware into the shared core behind an abstraction both hosts implement.
Put CI on the WordPress repositories: lint, type-check and a built artefact.
Add a nonce or signed-token check to the competition endpoint rather than relying on reCAPTCHA.
Introduce a form-definition schema so a new vertical is data rather than a new component tree.
Clean up the invalid indexes and consolidate the overlapping duplicate-check indexes.

Generate a correlation UUID in the browser at the start of every quote journey, send it with both the partial and final submission, and upsert on it in the lead API, reducing de-duplication to a fallback.

interview_stories.theme: Forensic debugging / challenging a metric (strongest story in the set)
interview_stories.situation: The production lead table showed a 33% duplicate rate — the kind of number that reads as a broken system.
interview_stories.task: Establish whether it was a defect, and what the real enquiry volume was.
interview_stories.action: Traced the partial-submission path in code and found no client-generated correlation ID. Measured gap distributions and found 94% of duplicates arriving within 30 minutes, 91% within five. Ran the control comparison: the form-driven channel showed 48.6% sub-30-minute repeats against 0.2-6.7% for single-post affiliate feeds.
interview_stories.result: Mechanism established, the platform's real figure restated as ~309,500 unique enquiries rather than 397,667 raw rows, and a bounded fix specified.
interview_stories.evidence: Gap-distribution and channel-comparison tables; nextHandler; send.php; leads schema
interview_stories.why_strong: Shows reading a system through its data rather than its code alone, using a control group to test a hypothesis, and arriving at a number that is lower but defensible.

interview_stories.situation: Dialler enrolment requires two SOAP calls against a system with 314 recorded connection failures.
interview_stories.action: Modelled three prior states (already queued, in flight, failed with no customer ID) and chose to return failed in the third case because the external outcome is unknown and a retry could create an uncleanable duplicate.
interview_stories.result: No duplicate CRM customers; recovery is an explicit decision.

interview_stories.result: Correct behaviour same-day and a changed process: confirm the rule before shipping.

audit_limitations: Commit counts measure activity, not impact; a one-line config commit and a 2,000-line feature count the same.
The leads table's earliest row is 2024-01-09, which bounds the measurable period but is not necessarily the system's first production day.
Four INVALID indexes on leads were observed, not investigated; nothing was changed.
Outcomes beyond lead ingestion (quotes produced, policies bound, revenue) are in systems not accessible from this database.
The competition wheel and register-interest form write to Azure endpoints outside this database; their production usage could not be measured.
No monitoring, logging or deployment telemetry was available, so no uptime, latency or deployment-frequency figures appear anywhere.
Causation is never claimed where only correlation is observable, notably the click-ID coverage change and the 2026 volume decline.

Unique-enquiry figures depend on a 30-minute collapse window, a judgement call. The gap distribution is concentrated enough (91% of repeats inside five minutes) that the result is stable across 10-60 minutes, but it cannot separate a partial-then-full pair from a genuine immediate resubmission, and one person with two phone numbers still counts twice.

No partial flag is persisted on the lead row, so partial and full submissions cannot be distinguished directly in the data; the diagnosis rests on code plus timing plus the cross-channel control, not on a stored field.

Employment start date (November 2024) was supplied by the subject and corroborated against the Git record, where all 384 commits fall on or after 1 Nov 2024. The exact start date within that month is not independently verifiable here.

audit_method.code: Six repositories inspected: structure, READMEs, package manifests, source, configuration, CI workflows, Dockerfile, full git log --all with authorship.
audit_method.database: PostgreSQL 16 production database connected with default_transaction_read_only = on and a statement timeout. All queries were SELECT with aggregate functions. No DDL, DML, migration or index operation was executed. No raw lead rows were retrieved.
audit_method.privacy: No credential, connection string, API key, token, customer name, phone number, email address or other personal datum appears in any output file.
audit_method.tenure_scoping: Career claims are scoped to created_at >= '2024-11-01'. Unique-enquiry counts use a window function partitioned by (mobile, type, source) ordered by created_at, counting rows whose gap to the previous row is null or >= 30 minutes.

key_finding_duplicate_diagnosis.headline: The 33% production duplicate rate is an architectural artifact of partial form submissions, not a data-quality failure.
key_finding_duplicate_diagnosis.mechanism: The multi-step quote form posts a partial submission mid-journey so drop-outs remain contactable, then posts again in full at the end. The second post carries no client-generated correlation ID, so the lead API cannot match it to the first and inserts a second row.
code_evidence: src/utils/index.ts nextHandler() calls submitForm(values, true) mid-journey and fires a partialSubmit dataLayer event
plugin/api/functions/send.php forwards a 'partial' boolean and suppresses notification email when true
leads table has no column for a client-supplied correlation ID
key_finding_duplicate_diagnosis.the_fix: Mint a UUID in the browser at the start of the journey, send it with both the partial and the final submission, and have the lead API upsert on it, retaining de-duplication as a fallback for sources that cannot supply one.
key_finding_duplicate_diagnosis.fix_already_half_built: The newer verticals the subject authored (Business Insurance, Landlord, Plant & Machinery, Fast Food) each generate a client-side uuidv4() as 'id' in their initial values. That id is forwarded on the Marketplace data-warehouse route but NOT on the main send route to the lead API, and the leads table has no column to receive it. Closing the loop is bounded work.
why_it_matters: Converts a metric that reads as a defect into evidence of analytical rigour
Produces honest headline figures (~309,500 unique enquiries) instead of inflated raw counts
Demonstrates engineering judgement: the problem was identified and the fix partly built before this audit
